items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend chapter 963 of the laws of 2021 amending the environmental
conservation law relating to supermarkets providing excess edible food to food
relief organizations, in relation to extending the effectiveness of certain
provisions thereof
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S6018

SPONSOR: HARCKHAM
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend chapter 963 of the laws of 2021 amending the environ-
mental conservation law relating to supermarkets providing excess edible
food to food relief organizations, in relation to extending the effec-
tiveness of certain provisions thereof

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is to extend the environmental conservation law
provisions that facilitate the donation of food from supermarkets to
food relief organizations and diverts edible excess food from landfills
that expires December 31, 2021.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill amends section 6 of chapter 63 of the laws of 2021
amending the environmental conservation law relating to supermarkets
providing excess edible food to food relief organizations by extending
the effectiveness of section four to December 31, 2026 at which time it
shall expire and be deemed repealed.

Section 2 is the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Hunger is a pervasive problem in America, and has been exacerbated by
the COVID-19 pandemic. An estimated 2.3 million New Yorkers face hunger
and food insecurity.

In recognition of this, in February 2021, the environmental conservation
law was amended to require retail supermarkets in excess of ten thousand
square feet to make available excess edible food to food relief organ-
izations if requested in writing under certain conditions. While such
supermarkets are required to participate, they are not required to
provide a specific quantity of food or transport and distribute such
food. This law will expire on December 31, 2021.

It was thought, at the time, that the food donation provisions would be
covered by Environmental Conservation Law Article 27- Food Donation and
Food Scraps Law enacted in the 2019 budget, effective as of January 1,
2022. However, this law will only require large food generators that
generate food scraps of two tons (4,000 pounds) or mote each week to
donate excess edible food and recycle all remaining food scraps. While
laudable in its goals, by making this law applicable to large food
generators only (higher educational institutions, hotels, correctional
facilities, large supermarkets and sports or entertainment venues),
local supermarkets in villages, towns, and counties throughout the State
will no longer be required to donate excess edible food as intended by
the law passed in 2021.

This legislation will extend for five years the excess edible food law
passed in 2021 and help ensure continued food donations to local and
community-based food relief organizations while also reducing the amount
of food waste diverted to solid waste landfills.

Making excess food available to local and community-based food relief
organizations will help address food insecurity in our state without
additional costs to participating supermarkets. Additionally; supermar-
kets that make excess food available as outlined in the initial legis-
lation receive the liability protections offered by the federal Bill
Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

This is new legislation

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately; and section four shall expire
December 31, 2026.

approvalMessage.text:
APPROVAL MEMORANDUM - No. 144 Chapter 791
 
       MEMORANDUM filed with Senate Bill Number 6018-B, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT  to amend chapter 63 of the laws of 2021 amending the envi-
        ronmental conservation law relating  to  supermarkets  providing
        excess  edible food to food relief organizations, in relation to
        extending the effectiveness of certain provisions thereof"
 
    APPROVED
 
  This bill will further extend a repeal date of a law adopted  in  2021
that  required supermarkets to provide excess edible food to food relief
organizations from time to time. The law sought to be extended  was  set
to expire on December 31, 2021, before the Food Donation and Food Scraps
Recycling  Law  (Food  Scraps Law) took effect January 1, 2022. The Food
Scraps Law, which was adopted in the 2019 Budget applies to persons  who
generate  an average of two tons per week or more of food scraps using a
methodology to be set in regulation by the Department  of  Environmental
Conservation  (DEC).  Designated food scraps generators will be required
under the Food Scraps Law to  separate  excess  food  for  donation  and
report  annually to the Department on the amount of food donated and the
amount transported for recycling.
 
  This bill, if extended beyond the December 31, 2021 repeal  date,  had
the  potential  to conflict with the Food Scraps Law as covered entities
were limited to supermarkets that exceeded a  square  footage  threshold
rather than tonnage requirement in the Food Scraps Law. In light of this
concern and the potential to cause ambiguity in the regulated community,
the  Executive  and  the Legislature have agreed to modify the law which
was set to expire to make it applicable to supermarkets who do not qual-
ify as a designated food scrap generator  under  the  Food  Scraps  Law.
These  changes should conceivably relieve any potential for conflict and
will continue to meet the sponsor's objective to encourage food donation
wherever practicable. On the basis of the  amendment  to  be  introduced
next session, I can approve this bill.
 
  This bill is approved.                         (signed) KATHY HOCHUL
 
                                ______
